hints: For particle Q moving up the incline, friction acts down the incline opposing motion.
Calculate the friction force: $F_Q = \mu R_Q = 0.6(12m) = 7.2m\text{ N}$.
Apply Newton's second law up the plane: $-2mg\sin\alpha - F_Q = 2ma_Q$, and solve for $a_Q$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the normal reaction on $Q$ ($m_Q = 2m$, $\sin\alpha = 0.8 \implies \cos\alpha = 0.6$):
$$R_Q = 2mg\cos\alpha = 2m(10)(0.6) = 12m\text{ N}$$

Calculate the friction force opposing upward motion using $\mu = 0.6$:
$$F_Q = \mu R_Q = 0.6(12m) = 7.2m\text{ N}$$

Calculate the component of weight acting down the incline:
$$W_{\parallel, Q} = 2mg\sin\alpha = 2m(10)(0.8) = 16m\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law up the plane:
$$-W_{\parallel, Q} - F_Q = 2ma_Q$$
$$-16m - 7.2m = 2ma_Q$$
$$-23.2m = 2ma_Q \implies a_Q = -\frac{23.2}{2} = -11.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Identify the forces acting on particle $Q$ of mass $2m$ moving up the incline:
- Normal reaction $R_Q$ perpendicular to the incline.
- Weight $2mg$ acting vertically downwards.
- Friction force $F_Q$ acting down the incline opposing the upward motion.

Resolve forces perpendicular to the incline:
$$R_Q = 2mg\cos\alpha$$
Using $\sin\alpha = 0.8$, we have $\cos\alpha = \sqrt{1 - 0.8^2} = 0.6$:
$$R_Q = 2m(10)(0.6) = 12m\text{ N}$$

Calculate the friction force using $F_Q = \mu R_Q$ with $\mu = 0.6$:
$$F_Q = 0.6(12m) = 7.2m\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law along the plane in the upward direction:
$$\sum F_\parallel = 2m a_Q$$
$$-2mg\sin\alpha - F_Q = 2m a_Q$$
Substitute $2mg\sin\alpha = 2m(10)(0.8) = 16m$ and $F_Q = 7.2m$:
$$-16m - 7.2m = 2m a_Q$$
$$-23.2m = 2m a_Q$$
Divide both sides by $2m$:
$$a_Q = -\frac{23.2m}{2m} = -11.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
Thus the acceleration of $Q$ up the plane is $-11.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$ as required.

hints: Find the downward acceleration of particle P: $mg\sin\alpha - 0.6(mg\cos\alpha) = ma_P \implies a_P = 4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Determine the time $t_{\text{stop}}$ for Q to come to instantaneous rest at its highest point using $v = 10 - 11.6t = 0 \implies t = \frac{25}{29}\text{ s}$.
Check whether they have collided by comparing the sum of their displacements at $t = \frac{25}{29}\text{ s}$ to the initial separation of $6.4\text{ m}$.
Show that Q begins sliding down with acceleration $4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$, so relative acceleration becomes zero, and find the additional time needed to close the remaining gap.
walkthrough:
Find the acceleration of $P$ sliding down the plane ($m_P = m$):
$$R_P = mg\cos\alpha = 6m,\quad F_P = 0.6(6m) = 3.6m$$
$$mg\sin\alpha - F_P = ma_P \implies 8m - 3.6m = ma_P \implies a_P = 4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Determine when $Q$ reaches instantaneous rest at the top of its ascent:
$$0 = 10 - 11.6 t_1 \implies t_1 = \frac{10}{11.6} = \frac{25}{29} \approx 0.86207\text{ s}$$

Calculate displacements at $t_1 = \frac{25}{29}\text{ s}$:
$$s_{Q,\text{up}} = \frac{10^2}{2(11.6)} = \frac{125}{29} \approx 4.31034\text{ m}$$
$$s_{P,\text{down}} = \frac{1}{2}(4.4)\left(\frac{25}{29}\right)^2 \approx 1.63496\text{ m}$$
$$\text{Combined distance} = 4.31034 + 1.63496 = 5.94530\text{ m} < 6.4\text{ m}$$

Because $2mg\sin\alpha = 16m > 7.2m = F_{\text{max}}$, $Q$ now accelerates down the plane:
$$2mg\sin\alpha - F_Q = 2m a_{Q,\text{down}} \implies 16m - 7.2m = 2m a_{Q,\text{down}} \implies a_{Q,\text{down}} = 4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

With both particles having the same downward acceleration ($4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$), relative speed is constant:
$$v_{\text{rel}} = v_P(t_1) = 4.4\left(\frac{25}{29}\right) \approx 3.7931\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$\Delta s = 6.4 - 5.94530 = 0.45470\text{ m}$$
$$t_2 = \frac{0.45470}{3.79310} \approx 0.11987\text{ s}$$
$$t_{\text{total}} = t_1 + t_2 = 0.86207 + 0.11987 = 0.982\text{ s}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
First, find the acceleration of particle $P$ sliding down from rest. The forces acting on $P$ parallel to the incline are:
- Component of gravity down the plane: $mg\sin\alpha = m(10)(0.8) = 8m$
- Friction force opposing motion up the plane: $F_P = \mu R_P = 0.6(mg\cos\alpha) = 0.6(m \times 10 \times 0.6) = 3.6m$
Apply Newton's second law down the plane:
$$8m - 3.6m = m a_P \implies a_P = 4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Find the time $t_1$ and distance $s_Q$ when $Q$ reaches the top of its ascent:
$$v_Q = u_Q + a_Q t_1 \implies 0 = 10 - 11.6 t_1 \implies t_1 = \frac{10}{11.6} = \frac{25}{29} \approx 0.86207\text{ s}$$
$$s_Q = \frac{u_Q^2}{2|a_Q|} = \frac{100}{2(11.6)} = \frac{125}{29} \approx 4.31034\text{ m}$$

Find the distance moved down the plane by $P$ in this time $t_1$:
$$s_P = \frac{1}{2}a_P t_1^2 = \frac{1}{2}(4.4)\left(\frac{25}{29}\right)^2 = 2.2\left(\frac{625}{841}\right) \approx 1.63496\text{ m}$$

Check whether collision has occurred: the sum of distances is $4.31034 + 1.63496 = 5.94530\text{ m}$. Since this is strictly less than the initial distance of $6.4\text{ m}$, the particles have not yet collided.

Analyse particle $Q$'s downward motion: the component of weight down the plane is $16m$, which exceeds limiting friction $7.2m$, so $Q$ accelerates downwards:
$$a_{Q,\text{down}} = \frac{16m - 7.2m}{2m} = \frac{8.8m}{2m} = 4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
Because both particles now accelerate downwards at the same rate of $4.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$, their relative acceleration is zero.

Calculate the time $t_2$ to close the remaining gap $\Delta s = 6.4 - 5.94530 = 0.45470\text{ m}$ at relative speed $v_{\text{rel}} = v_P(t_1) = 4.4\left(\frac{25}{29}\right) = \frac{110}{29} \approx 3.79310\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$t_2 = \frac{\Delta s}{v_{\text{rel}}} = \frac{0.45470}{3.79310} \approx 0.11987\text{ s}$$

Add the time intervals to get the total time before collision:
$$t_{\text{total}} = t_1 + t_2 = 0.86207 + 0.11987 = 0.98194\text{ s}$$
Rounding to three significant figures gives:
$$t = 0.982\text{ s}$$
Thus the time for which the particles are in motion before they collide is $0.982\text{ s}$.

hints: Find the speed of P immediately before impact using $v_P = 4.4 \times 0.982\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Find the speed of Q immediately before impact using $v_Q = 4.4 \times 0.120\text{ m s}^{-1}$ down the plane.
Both particles are moving down the plane immediately before impact.
Apply conservation of linear momentum: $m v_P + 2m v_Q = 3m V$, and solve for the combined speed $V$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the speeds of $P$ and $Q$ directed down the plane at the moment of collision ($t = 0.982\text{ s}$):
$$v_P = 4.4(0.982) = 4.3208\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$v_Q = 4.4(0.982 - 0.862) = 4.4(0.120) = 0.528\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Apply conservation of linear momentum down the plane for the coalescence into mass $3m$:
$$m(4.3208) + 2m(0.528) = 3m V$$
$$4.3208 + 1.056 = 3V$$
$$5.3768 = 3V$$
$$V = \frac{5.3768}{3} \approx 1.79\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Calculate the downward velocities of particles $P$ and $Q$ immediately before collision:
- Particle $P$ has been accelerating down the plane from rest for the full duration $t = 0.982\text{ s}$:
$$v_P = a_P t = (4.4)(0.982) = 4.3208\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
- Particle $Q$ has been accelerating down the plane from rest at its apex for duration $t_2 = 0.982 - 0.86207 = 0.11993\text{ s}$:
$$v_Q = a_{Q,\text{down}} t_2 = (4.4)(0.120) = 0.528\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Notice that both particles are moving down the slope at the moment of impact.

State the principle of conservation of linear momentum along the plane:
$$m_P v_P + m_Q v_Q = (m_P + m_Q)V$$

Substitute the masses $m_P = m$, $m_Q = 2m$, and combined mass $3m$:
$$m(4.3208) + 2m(0.528) = 3m V$$
Divide both sides by $m$:
$$4.3208 + 2(0.528) = 3V$$
$$4.3208 + 1.056 = 3V$$
$$5.3768 = 3V$$
Divide both sides by $3$:
$$V = \frac{5.3768}{3} \approx 1.79227\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Rounding to three significant figures gives:
$$V = 1.79\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Thus the speed of the combined particle immediately after the impact is $1.79\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
